I published my first Atlantic Canada Small-Business Opportunity Report this week.

I build custom software, and now custom AI-based tools, for small service businesses in Kentville, so I spend most days inside the admin side of small firms: the quoting, the scheduling, the invoices at 9 pm. I wanted to see what the data says about the region from that vantage point. Three findings stood out.

1. Succession. 76% of Canadian small business owners plan to exit within ten years, and 9% have a formal plan (CFIB). 39% of businesses are too reliant on their owner to be sellable.

2. Admin time. Canadian small businesses spent 735 hours on regulatory compliance per business in 2024 (CFIB).

3. Trades. Vacancies for trades, transport and equipment operators rose for the first time since 2022, to about 92,600 in Q4 2025 (Statistics Canada).

The thread through all three: when the process lives in the owner’s head, or inside software nobody chose, the business is harder to hand over, to hire into and to run. Off-the-shelf software makes you learn its words and its process. I think the better default is to build the software around how the business already works.

Every number in the report has its source. Where I couldn’t verify something, I said so.

Job description of the week: dishwasher, Nova Scotia edition.

The job that keeps the kitchen open. What to put in the ad:

1. The pay. Nova Scotia’s minimum wage is $17.00 an hour since October 1, 2026. If you pay more, put the number in the ad.
2. What the shift looks like (an example split from our template): warewashing, pots and pans, the dish machine, garbage and organics, chemicals, restocking.
3. Food hygiene. Under Nova Scotia’s Food Safety Regulations, anyone who comes into contact with food must be trained or instructed in food hygiene to a level that fits their job.
4. WHMIS. Dish machine detergent and sanitizer are hazardous products; workers who use them need WHMIS training, reviewed at least once a year.
5. Hiring someone under 16? At 14 or 15 they can work in a restaurant if they don’t operate cooking equipment and get proper safety training and supervision. Under 14: no work between 10 pm and 6 am, and no more than 3 hours on a school day without a certificate.
